about: Source of Pray the Psalms (/tools/pray-the-psalms), written by hand. Each psalm has the kinds the Study Bible's notes give it (with the note's own words as evidence, in src, or through a group a note names), the times of life it fits (when), one line on what it prays and a short guide to praying it, both written to agree with the psalm's plain note (client/public/bible/notes/psalms/plain/<n>.json), and the paragraphs of that plain note to show word for word (care, ending). No verse is typed here: scripts/build-pray-psalms.mjs fills every psalm from the BSB and copies each note's title and summary word for word.

kinds.name: Lament
kinds.line: Trouble brought straight to God: a call, the complaint, a plea, and often a turn toward trust.

kinds.name: Lament of the people
kinds.line: The whole people's cry to God in a time of disaster.

kinds.name: Thanksgiving
kinds.line: Telling how God rescued someone, so that others can praise him too.

src: Songs of thanksgiving tell how God rescued someone, so that others can praise him too (Psalms 30, 34, 116).

kinds.name: Praise
kinds.line: A song of praise for who God is and what he has made.

src: Songs of praise, or hymns, praise God for who he is and what he has made (Psalms 8, 100, 104).
After a long run of laments and trust psalms (51 to 64), it opens a group of four songs of praise (65 to 68) that celebrate God's rule over creation and the nations.
on to a final crescendo in which every psalm from 146 to 150 begins and ends with Hallelujah, praise the LORD.

kinds.name: Trust
kinds.line: A prayer that rests in God's care.

src: Psalms of trust rest in God's care (Psalms 23, 27, 91, 131).
Psalm 64 closes the small group of Davidic trust psalms in 61 to 64 and is the last lament before the three great songs of praise in Psalms 65 to 67.

kinds.name: Wisdom
kinds.line: Teaching, like the book of Proverbs: two ways to live, and why the wicked often do well.

src: Wisdom psalms teach, like the book of Proverbs. They set out two ways to live and wrestle with why the wicked often do well (Psalms 1, 37, 49, 73, 112).

kinds.name: Royal
kinds.line: About Israel's king: his crowning, his wedding, his battles, and God's promise to his family.

src: Royal psalms are about the king of Israel: his crowning, his wedding, his battles, God's promise to his family (Psalms 2, 18, 20, 21, 45, 72, 89, 101, 110, 132, 144).

kinds.name: The LORD reigns
kinds.line: Celebrating the LORD as King over all the earth.

src: It is one of the enthronement psalms, a group (usually 47, 93, and 95 to 99) that celebrate the LORD as king.

kinds.name: Song of Zion
kinds.line: Celebrating Zion, the city of God, as the place of his presence.

kinds.name: Israel's story
kinds.line: Retelling Israel's history so that the next generation remembers what God has done.

src: Psalm 78 is the second longest psalm (after Psalm 119) and the first of several historical psalms that retell Israel's story (compare Psalms 105, 106, and 136).

kinds.name: Liturgy
kinds.line: Words for worship at the sanctuary, often with more than one voice.

kinds.name: Penitential
kinds.line: One of the seven psalms the church has prayed in times of repentance.

src: From early in Christian history the church grouped Psalm 6 with Psalms 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, and 143 as the seven Penitential Psalms, prayed especially in times of repentance and during Lent.

kinds.name: Cursing psalm
kinds.line: A prayer that calls down judgment on enemies, often called imprecatory. Spoken to God, never a command to people.

src: It belongs to a group of psalms often called imprecatory, meaning psalms that call down curses or judgment on enemies (others include Psalms 35, 69, 109, and 137).

kinds.name: Song of ascents
kinds.line: One of fifteen short songs, Psalms 120 to 134, that many think pilgrims sang going up to Jerusalem.

src: Psalm 120 opens the Songs of Ascents, a collection of fifteen short psalms (120 to 134) that each carry the heading

whens.name: Afraid
whens.line: Fear that will not settle.

whens.name: Under threat
whens.line: Real danger, or people set against you.

whens.name: Grieving
whens.line: A death, a loss, a hope gone.

whens.name: Guilty
whens.line: Something done that needs forgiving.

whens.name: Angry with God, or asking why
whens.line: When God seems absent, silent or unfair.

whens.name: Betrayed or falsely accused
whens.line: Hurt by someone close, or by lies.

whens.name: Alone
whens.line: No one near, or no one who understands.

whens.name: Far from God
whens.line: Dry, distant or wandering.

whens.name: Awake in the night
whens.line: Sleepless, or afraid of the dark hours.

whens.name: Sick or in pain
whens.line: Illness in the body, or strength worn down.

whens.name: Growing old, or facing death
whens.line: The shortness of life, and the hope beyond it.

whens.name: Watching wrong win
whens.line: Envy of the wicked, or anger at injustice.

whens.name: Waiting
whens.line: For an answer that has not come yet.

whens.name: At a loss for words
whens.line: Short prayers, and words to borrow when yours run out.

whens.name: Thankful
whens.line: Something given, or a rescue to tell.

whens.name: Full of praise
whens.line: Joy that wants to sing.

whens.name: Wanting to live wisely
whens.line: Choices, habits and the way to walk.

whens.name: Starting the day
whens.line: A psalm to begin with.

whens.name: Ending the day
whens.line: A psalm to lie down with.

whens.name: Before worship
whens.line: Coming into God's presence with his people.

psalms.line: Blesses the person rooted in God's instruction, like a tree by streams of water, and sets that life beside the way that blows away like chaff.
psalms.guide: Read the three verbs of verse 1 and ask where drifting has already become sitting in your own life. Then ask what you are rooted near. The psalm does not tell you to try harder; it tells you to stay close to the water, so read a few lines of Scripture slowly and return to them through the day.

psalms.line: The nations plot against the LORD and his anointed king, God answers from heaven by installing his King on Zion, and the psalm ends with a blessing on all who take refuge in him.
psalms.guide: Ask where the old wish to throw off God's rule lives quietly in you. When the world seems to rage against what is good, pray it as the first Christians did, for courage rather than revenge. End where the psalm ends, with its open door to everyone who runs to God's king for refuge.

psalms.line: David, fleeing his own son, hears voices say God will not rescue him, answers that the LORD is his shield, and lies down and wakes again in safety.
psalms.guide: Notice the voice that says God will not deliver you, and make the psalm's turn: stop arguing with it and speak to God instead. Tonight, name to God what you fear and hand it over. The psalm ends by saying that salvation is the LORD's work, not yours.

trust: The psalm is an individual prayer of trust

psalms.line: An evening prayer: David asks to be answered, tells those who chase lies to be still and trust the LORD, and lies down in peace because God keeps him safe.
psalms.guide: Use it to end a hard day: lie still, look honestly at your own heart, and trust God with what you cannot fix. If sleep will not come, pray verse 8 slowly, more than once. If sleeplessness goes on for weeks, seeing a doctor is wise and is no failure of faith.

lament: The psalm is an individual lament and petition

psalms.line: A morning prayer at the door of God's house, laid before the holy God who will not welcome evil, asking him to lead the one praying straight through a world of lies.
psalms.guide: Begin tomorrow early, before the day fills up: set your requests before God in order, then watch for his answer. Remember how the psalmist got in the door, by God's loving devotion and not his own goodness. Before you pray against those who lie about you, ask where your own words have done harm, then pray verse 8.

psalms.line: A man weak in body and shaken in soul begs God for mercy and healing, weeps through the night, and then, suddenly, knows that the LORD has heard his weeping.
psalms.guide: The psalm lets you ask God how long and leave the sentence unfinished; that is prayer too. Pray it as it is, without dressing it up, for yourself or for someone you love who cannot pray it tonight. Say verse 9 aloud, even before you feel it.

psalms.line: Hunted and falsely accused, David takes his case to God the righteous judge, asks to be judged by his integrity, and ends in thanks.
psalms.guide: When you are accused of what you did not do, take the case to God and let him judge rather than fighting back. Before you pray the dangerous words of verses 3 to 5, look hard at your own hands. Bring what could grow into harm to God while it is still small, as verse 14 warns.

psalms.line: Praise for the LORD whose name is majestic in all the earth, and wonder that the maker of moon and stars cares for human beings and crowns them with glory.
psalms.guide: Go outside on a clear night and ask the psalm's question about yourself. Let both answers settle: you are small, and you are crowned. Then ask how you are caring for the people, creatures and land put into your hands, since a crown given by God is a trust.

thanks: Psalm 9 leans toward thanksgiving and confidence

psalms.line: Whole-hearted thanks to the LORD who judges justly and does not forget the afflicted, then a prayer for mercy in present trouble.
psalms.guide: Before you ask God for anything, recount one thing he has already done. If you feel forgotten, hold on to verse 18: it does not promise the wait will be short, only that it will not be forever. If you have power over others, let verse 20 remind you that you are only human.

lament: The psalm moves from lament to confidence

psalms.line: Asks why the LORD stands far off while the poor are hunted, paints the man who says God never sees, and ends trusting the King who helps the fatherless.
psalms.guide: If you are hurt and God seems far away, the first verse gives you words to pray. Ask also where the voice that says God never sees has crept into your own choices. When cruelty goes unpunished, pray verse 12, then ask whom near you you could stand beside.

trust: Psalm 11 is a psalm of trust

psalms.line: Urged to flee like a bird when the foundations shake, David stays, because the LORD is still on his throne and sees everyone.
psalms.guide: The psalm does not say running is always wrong; David ran from Saul more than once. It asks where your real refuge is when the ground shakes. When the news leaves you asking what the righteous can do, pray verse 4 slowly, then do the next right thing in front of you.

people: The psalm is a community lament

psalms.line: A cry for help when the faithful seem gone and everyone lies and flatters, answered by God's promise to rise for the oppressed and by his words, pure as refined silver.
psalms.guide: Watch your own words: is there a double heart in how you speak, kind to a face and cruel behind a back? When it seems no one can be trusted, ask the LORD for help as verse 1 does, and rest on his word. The psalm ends with the trouble not yet over, and trusts anyway.

lament: Psalm 13 is a textbook example of the lament form

psalms.line: Four times David asks how long God will forget him, then, with nothing yet changed, sets his trust in God's loving devotion and promises to sing.
psalms.guide: Asking how long four times over is not a lack of faith; it is faith arguing with a God it still believes is there. Pray all six verses. If you cannot yet say verse 5 for yourself, say it as the church's words, and let them wait in you until they become your own.

wisdom: Psalm 14 blends wisdom reflection with prophetic accusation and communal lament

psalms.line: The fool lives as if God will never judge; the LORD looks down and finds that all have turned aside, yet he stands with the righteous and shelters the poor.
psalms.guide: Ask where you live as if God does not see; most believers keep rooms like that. Then pray verse 7 for everyone who waits for God to put things right.

liturgy: Many scholars classify Psalm 15 as an entrance liturgy

psalms.line: Asks who may dwell on God's holy mountain, and answers with a portrait of a trustworthy life: true speech, promises kept when they cost, honest money.
psalms.guide: Read the list slowly and ask which line is hardest for you. The psalm does not ask you to be impressive; it asks you to be trustworthy. Pray it as a request to be made that kind of guest in God's house.

trust: Psalm 16 is a psalm of trust and confession

psalms.line: David confesses he has no good apart from the LORD, his portion and inheritance, and trusts God to show him the path of life rather than abandon him to the grave.
psalms.guide: Ask what you count on to make life good, then pray verse 5 as your own; some days you will mean it fully, and some days it will be a prayer to come to mean it. Practise verse 8 as a daily habit. If you are grieving someone who trusted Christ, verse 11 is a verse to hold.

lament: The psalm is an individual lament

psalms.line: Surrounded and hunted, David asks God to hear a just cause, to keep him as the apple of his eye, and ends wanting God's face more than anything this life gives.
psalms.guide: When you are falsely accused, take the case to God rather than fighting it out in anger. Ask what your portion is, this life's goods or God's face. Pray verse 8 for yourself, or for a child, in the words of a parent guarding what they love most.

thanks: The psalm is a royal thanksgiving song

psalms.line: David's song of the day God came down in storm and fire and drew him out of deep waters, with praise for the Rock who equips and keeps his king.
psalms.guide: Begin where David begins, with love before requests, and name what God has been to you. When your own lamp is low, pray verse 28; it asks for light enough for the next step. Then pray verse 50 for those who will come after you.

praise: Psalm 19 is a hymn in two halves

psalms.line: The silent sky tells God's glory, his law is perfect and sweeter than honey, and the psalm ends asking to be cleansed of hidden faults.
psalms.guide: Look up and let the sky speak. Then ask whether God's word is treasure to you, or homework. Pray verse 14 before you speak today, in a hard meeting, at the table, before you post; it covers what you say and what you think.

psalms.line: The people pray for their king in the day of trouble, and the psalm sets those who trust in chariots and horses against those who trust the name of the LORD.
psalms.guide: Name your own chariots: money, health, skill, a plan. None of them is evil; the psalm asks what you trust when trouble comes. Use it to pray for leaders by name, before their hard days.

thanks: The psalm is a royal thanksgiving

psalms.line: Thanks that God has given the king his heart's desire, a look ahead to God's victory over his enemies, and an ending that praises God's strength rather than the king's.
psalms.guide: Psalm 20 asked and this one thanks: come back to thank God when the trouble passes, not only before it. Let every success end the way this psalm does, with praise for God.

lament: Modern scholarship classifies the psalm as an individual lament that turns into a song of thanksgiving
thanks: Modern scholarship classifies the psalm as an individual lament that turns into a song of thanksgiving

psalms.line: A sufferer who feels forsaken, mocked and laid in the dust is answered at the lowest point, and the psalm ends in praise that reaches the ends of the earth. Jesus prayed its first line from the cross.
psalms.guide: It gives you words for the worst moment of faith, when God seems gone, and you are allowed to say them. Remember what God did for others and for you, as verses 4, 9 and 10 do; memory does not take the pain away, but it gives the pain somewhere to go. Do not skip the first half to reach the second.

psalms.line: The LORD as a shepherd who feeds, leads and restores, present in the darkest valley, and as a host who spreads a table while enemies look on.
psalms.guide: Read it as a sheep reads it, as someone who needs looking after. Ask where you are today, in the pasture, on the path or in the valley; the psalm is true in all three. If you are grieving, it does not ask you to feel calm: read it slowly and let the shepherd be with you where you are.

liturgy: many scholars read it as a processional liturgy with alternating voices

psalms.line: The earth is the LORD's; who may climb his hill? Those with clean hands and a pure heart. Then the ancient gates are told to lift their heads for the King of glory.
psalms.guide: Hold what you have loosely, since it belongs to God first. Ask what you lift your soul to. Pray verses 7 to 10 aloud with others, as it was first sung: one voice calling, another asking, everyone answering.

psalms.line: A prayer that lifts the soul to God: teach me your ways, remember your loving devotion and not the sins of my youth, and turn to me in my loneliness.
psalms.guide: Ask what you would like God to forget; the psalm says you may ask, and that he remembers you by his loving devotion, not by your past. If you are lonely, verse 16 gives you words without dressing loneliness up as something else.

lament: often grouped with the individual laments, though it contains little complaint

psalms.line: Falsely accused, the psalmist asks God to test him and vindicate him, refuses the company of the deceitful, and ends blessing the LORD among his people.
psalms.guide: Say plainly to God that you did not do what you are accused of, and leave the verdict with him. Then ask about your company, and whether you love the place where God's people gather or only put up with it.

psalms.line: Bold trust that will not fear an army, one desire to dwell with God and see his beauty, then urgent prayer not to be forsaken, ending with a call to wait for the LORD.
psalms.guide: If you could ask God for one thing, what would it be? Sit with verse 4; prayer can be simply looking. Verse 8 is a good morning prayer. The psalm ends before the answer comes and tells you twice to wait, because once is rarely enough.

lament: The psalm is an individual lament with a turn to thanksgiving

psalms.line: The psalmist begs God not to be silent, asks not to be dragged away with those who speak peace and plan harm, and then praises: God has heard.
psalms.guide: If God's silence frightens you, say so and keep calling. Trust can speak before the proof arrives, as verse 6 does. When God has heard you, pray verse 9 for his whole people.

praise: The psalm is a hymn in three movements

psalms.line: The voice of the LORD thunders over the waters and breaks the cedars; God sits enthroned over the flood, and he gives his people strength and peace.
psalms.guide: Let creation make you small in a good way; when a storm shakes the windows, pray verse 3. Notice the ending: the God of the thunder uses his strength to give strength and his power to give peace.

psalms.line: A man brought back from near death thanks the LORD who healed him, admits he once thought he could never be shaken, and praises the God who turned his mourning into dancing.
psalms.guide: Remember a time God brought you through, and say it aloud to others; thanks shared becomes someone else's hope. Then ask what you trusted when things were easy, and answer before the next hard time comes.

lament: It belongs to the many laments of Book I of the Psalter

psalms.line: A man hunted, worn by grief and left by his friends commits his spirit into God's hands, and ends urging the faithful to be strong and hope in the LORD. Jesus prayed its fifth verse as he died.
psalms.guide: Pray verse 5 tonight before you sleep; it is a prayer for the end of a day and for the end of a life. On days when life feels out of control, say verse 15 slowly: your times are in God's hands, not in anyone else's.

psalms.line: The happiness of the forgiven: David tells what hiding his sin did to him, how quickly God forgave when he confessed, and how God became his hiding place.
psalms.guide: If you are keeping silent about something, the psalm does not shame you; it tells you what silence costs and what confession gives. Notice how quickly forgiveness follows confession in verse 5. Pray verse 7 slowly, then name what you are hiding from and let God be the place you hide.

praise: It is a hymn, a song of praise sung by the community

psalms.line: A call to sing a new song to the LORD, whose word made the heavens and whose counsel outlasts the plans of nations, and on whom his people wait.
psalms.guide: Name what you hope in; verses 16 and 17 list armies and horses, and yours might be savings, health or a plan. None of them is evil, and none of them saves. Then sing: a new song is praise that comes fresh because you have seen God at work again.

wisdom: It is a psalm of praise and a wisdom psalm at once

psalms.line: David praises the LORD who delivered him from all his fears, invites others to taste and see, and teaches the fear of the LORD: guard the tongue, seek peace, and know that God is near the brokenhearted.
psalms.guide: Thanks can come from humiliating places; David learned this pretending to be mad in an enemy city. The psalm asks you to try trusting God and find out. If you feel crushed, read verse 18 again: God comes near to the broken before they are strong.

lament: It is a lament of an individual

psalms.line: A man repaid evil for good asks the LORD to fight for him and plead his case; he had mourned for his accusers when they were sick, and they gloated when he stumbled.
psalms.guide: If someone you cared for has turned against you, the psalm gives words for that pain and lets you hand the case to God instead of fighting it yourself. Notice verse 13: before he prayed against them, he had prayed for them.

wisdom: many classify it as a mixture of wisdom reflection and lament

psalms.line: A portrait of the man who flatters himself and plots evil even in bed, set against the LORD whose loving devotion reaches the heavens and in whose light we see light.
psalms.guide: Ask what you are looking at, your own schemes or God. Verse 2 is a warning, so ask God to show you the sins you have stopped noticing.

psalms.line: An old man's counsel not to fret or envy when the wicked prosper: trust, delight, commit, be still and wait, for the future belongs to those who keep the LORD's way.
psalms.guide: Name the person or the unfairness that keeps you burning inside; the psalm does not say it does not matter, only that your anger will not fix it. Try verse 7 for a week; stillness is refusing to be pushed by envy. If you have gone hungry, it asks the rest of God's people to be the open hand that feeds you.

psalms.line: A man sick in body and crushed by guilt asks not to be rebuked in anger, names his wounds and the friends who stand far off, confesses, and ends with a short cry for help.
psalms.guide: It lets you be honest about pain and about sin at the same time, without pretending either is small. It also asks something of the healthy: who do you know who is ill and alone? Do not stand far off.

lament: It is one of the most searching laments in the Psalter

psalms.line: A man who tried to keep silent breaks into prayer, asks to know how short his life is, confesses that every person is only a breath, and ends without resolution.
psalms.guide: Count your days honestly, not to frighten yourself but to stop rushing after what will not last. Then ask the question of verse 7 about where your hope is. The psalm ends unresolved, and you may pray it as it is.

thanks: It is two kinds of psalm joined together: a thanksgiving (verses 1 to 10) and a lament (verses 11 to 17)
lament: It is two kinds of psalm joined together: a thanksgiving (verses 1 to 10) and a lament (verses 11 to 17)

psalms.line: David remembers waiting patiently until God drew him out of the pit and gave him a new song, offers himself to do God's will, and then, in trouble again, asks God not to delay.
psalms.guide: Tell where you have been lifted out of the mud, so that others may trust. If you are still waiting, keep waiting on God and not on what cannot hold your weight. The psalm ends with the problem unsolved; pray as it does, thankful for past rescues and honest that you need another.

psalms.line: A blessing on the one who cares for the poor, then a sick man's prayer while enemies wait for his death and a trusted friend turns on him; Book One closes in praise.
psalms.guide: Care for the poor and the sick, and visit without gossiping afterward, as verse 6 warns. If a friend has betrayed you, the psalm gives words for that wound, and Jesus has been there before you.

psalms.line: Far from the temple, a worshiper thirsts for God like a deer for water, hears people ask where his God is, and talks back to his own downcast soul: hope in God.
psalms.guide: Do what verse 5 does: ask your low soul why it is so low, then tell it where to look. That is not pretending to be fine; it is choosing where to look while you are still low. Hope is said again and again, so read on into Psalm 43, which finishes the poem.

lament: The psalm is an individual lament

psalms.line: The end of the poem begun in Psalm 42: a prayer for God's light and truth to lead him back to the altar, and the refrain again, telling his downcast soul to hope in God.
psalms.guide: If you read Psalm 42 and stopped, read this one too; the refrain is the same, but now he faces forward and asks to be led. Notice the name he gives God in verse 4, and pray it before the way back has opened.

people: Psalm 44 is the Psalter's boldest communal lament

psalms.line: The people remember God's past rescues, insist they have kept faith, and still cry for God to wake up and redeem them for the sake of his loving devotion.
psalms.guide: It gives you leave to argue with God when you have tried to be faithful and life has still fallen apart. Every line is spoken to him. Notice that the last words ask him to act for the sake of his loving devotion, not because anyone deserves it.

psalms.line: A court poet's song for the king's wedding day, praising his truth, humility and justice, then turning to the bride and her procession into the palace.
psalms.guide: Before the gold, the poet praises the king for truth, humility and justice. Christians who read it of Jesus are asked to picture him that way, and to hear in the bride that they are wanted, not merely put up with.

psalms.line: God is his people's refuge and strength, so they will not fear though the earth give way; he is within his city, and he calls them to be still and know that he is God.
psalms.guide: The psalm does not promise that nothing bad will happen; it says who is with you when it does. Say verse 1 into whatever your falling mountain is. Being still means letting go of control, so ask what you are gripping that God is asking you to drop.

praise: The two halves follow the typical pattern of a hymn

psalms.line: All peoples are called to clap and shout, because the LORD Most High is King over all the earth; it ends with the nobles of the nations gathered as the people of the God of Abraham.
psalms.guide: The hope here is not that one people wins and others lose, but that all of them end up praising the same King. Not every prayer is quiet; praise God aloud with others.

psalms.line: Praise for the LORD in Zion, the city that kings fled from; the worshipers walk around it and count its towers so they can tell the next generation that this God is their God forever.
psalms.guide: Look closely at what God has done so that you can pass it on. Ask who your next generation is, a child, a younger friend, someone new to faith, and what you could show them.

psalms.line: A teacher's riddle for rich and poor alike: no amount of money can ransom a life from death, but God will redeem the psalmist's life and take him to himself.
psalms.guide: The psalm is not against money but against trusting it; ask what you are counting on that death will take away. Hold what you own the way someone holds a thing they will have to leave.

psalms.line: God summons his people to court: he needs none of their sacrifices, he wants thanks, kept vows and prayer in trouble, and he warns those who recite his words while ignoring him.
psalms.guide: God needs nothing from you, and that is freeing: you cannot keep him going with your religion. Ask what you give him as if he needed it, and thank him instead. The warning is for people who know their Bibles, and it ends with an open door for anyone who turns.

psalms.line: David's plea for mercy after his sin with Bathsheba: confession without excuse, a prayer to be washed and made new, and the broken and contrite heart God will not despise.
psalms.guide: Pray it with no excuse in it, naming the wrong and leaning your whole weight on God's mercy. Ask, as verse 10 does, to be changed as well as forgiven. If you fear you have gone too far, remember who first prayed it.

psalms.line: David confronts a powerful man who used his tongue like a razor, and pictures himself as an olive tree flourishing in the house of God.
psalms.guide: Ask what your words are for: to build up or to devour. Then look at the two trees, one uprooted for trusting wealth, the other growing for trusting God's loving devotion, and ask where your roots are.

psalms.line: Psalm 14 again: the fool's quiet thought that God does not matter, a humanity gone corrupt, and a longing for rescue to come from Zion.
psalms.guide: The fool's thought is not only a skeptic's; it lies behind much of ordinary life, in church as well as out of it. Read it beside Psalm 14, and pray it as a longing for God's rescue.

lament: Psalm 54 is one of the shortest laments in the Psalter

psalms.line: Betrayed by people who should have protected him, David asks God to save him by his name, declares God his helper, and promises a freewill offering of thanks.
psalms.guide: This short psalm moves from fear to trust in seven verses, turning at verse 4. Its prayer against enemies is left to God, not acted out. Let it end where it ends, in a gift given freely.

lament: The psalm is an individual lament

psalms.line: Terrified, the psalmist wishes for wings like a dove to fly away; his deepest wound is a close friend's betrayal, and he calls on God evening, morning and noon.
psalms.guide: The wish to run is honest, and sometimes stepping away is wise, but he tells God about it and keeps praying. A friend's betrayal hurts more than an enemy's attack, and your pain is no overreaction. Then do with the weight you carry what verse 22 says.

lament: The psalm is an individual lament that turns into thanksgiving

psalms.line: Hounded by enemies who twist his words, David answers his own fear with trust, and believes that God keeps count of every tear.
psalms.guide: Verse 3 does not say you will never be afraid; fear comes, and trust is what you do with it. Verse 8 is for anyone who has cried where no one saw: tell God about each tear.

psalms.line: Hiding in a cave from Saul, David shelters in the shadow of God's wings while enemies surround him like lions, and wakes his harp to praise at dawn.
psalms.guide: The praise starts in the cave, before the danger has passed. A steadfast heart is steady because God is, not calm because things are fine. Try waking the dawn with praise tomorrow while the trouble is still there.

cursing: It belongs to a group of psalms often called imprecatory

psalms.line: David confronts rulers who pervert justice and asks God to break the power of the wicked, ending with the confession that there is a God who judges the earth.
psalms.guide: It is a cry from people crushed by those meant to protect them, not a pattern for how to feel about people you dislike. If you have been wronged like that, bring your anger to God in words as strong as you need, and leave the judging to him. If you hold any power over others, its first question is for you.

psalms.line: With killers watching his house, David asks God to deliver him from men who prowl like dogs at night, and sings of God's strength in the morning.
psalms.guide: Many people lie awake while fears prowl. The psalm does not promise the dogs will vanish; it tells you to watch for God, as verse 9 does, and promises that morning will come. Say verse 16 to yourself at night and see if it is true at dawn.

psalms.line: After a defeat the people cry that God has rejected them; God answers from his sanctuary, and the psalm ends trusting that with God they will act with valor.
psalms.guide: It teaches a people what to do after a defeat: tell God the truth, listen for his promise, and go on with him. Ask where you have been broken, and pray verse 12 there.

psalms.line: From the ends of the earth, with a fainting heart, the psalmist asks to be led to a rock higher than he can climb, and longs to shelter in God's tent.
psalms.guide: When your heart is faint you cannot lift yourself; you need something firmer than you are, and someone to lead you to it. Pray verse 2 from wherever the ends of the earth are for you, and let verse 8 show the answer: faithfulness day by day, not all at once.

psalms.line: David waits quietly for God alone, his rock and fortress, while enemies try to topple him with lies, and calls the people to pour out their hearts to God.
psalms.guide: Rest here means stopping the inner struggle and trusting God with it, and the psalmist has to tell his own soul to do it. Take the invitation of verse 8 and pour out everything, not tidy prayers. Then ask what you lean your heart on that weighs less than a breath.

psalms.line: In a dry and weary land David thirsts for God, finds his loving devotion better than life, and remembers him through the watches of the night.
psalms.guide: If you feel dry toward God, that longing is itself a kind of prayer. Pray verses 1 to 5 first thing in the morning, as Christians have for many centuries. If you lie awake, use the hours to remember what God has done; your grip on him may feel weak, but his grip on you is not.

psalms.line: David asks to be hidden from schemers whose words fly like arrows from ambush; God shoots back, and the righteous take refuge in him.
psalms.guide: If you have been hurt by gossip or lies, tell God how sharp the words were; hidden plans are not hidden from him, and you do not have to fire back. Then ask whether your own words have ever been arrows.

psalms.line: Praise waits for God in Zion, who hears prayer and atones for sin, stills the seas and the nations, and crowns the year with a harvest so rich the hills seem to sing.
psalms.guide: Notice the order: forgiveness, then creation, then harvest. The God who makes the wheat grow is the God who deals with our sin. Next time you eat bread, remember verse 11, and thank the giver of rain, soil, seed and sun.

psalms.line: All the earth is called to come and see what God has done, from the sea made dry land to a people refined by fire and water, and one worshiper tells how God heard his prayer.
psalms.guide: Faith is a shared story and a personal one; the psalm moves from what God did for everyone to what he did for one person. Is there something God has brought you through that someone else needs to hear? Thanks said aloud helps others believe.

psalms.line: A prayer for God to be gracious and make his face shine on his people, so that his salvation will be known among all nations and all peoples praise him.
psalms.guide: Ask why you want God's blessing: for your own comfort, or so that others see what he is like. Verse 7 joins the two. Ask who around you could see God's kindness through what he has given you.

psalms.line: God arises and his enemies scatter; he is father of the fatherless and defender of widows, who settles the lonely in families and daily bears his people's burden.
psalms.guide: If you grew up without a father, or feel alone, verses 5 and 6 are for you, and God often settles the lonely through his people. Learn verse 19: you do not carry your load alone, today or tomorrow. If you have a home, ask whom you could make room for.

lament: It is one of the longest individual laments in the book

psalms.line: A sufferer sinking in deep waters cries for rescue; hated without cause and shunned by his own family, he finds no comforter, calls down judgment, and ends in praise while still in pain.
psalms.guide: Begin where the psalm begins, with the cry for God to save you; that is enough to start. Verse 20 is one of the loneliest lines in the Bible, and it asks the rest of us to be the comforter he could not find. If you are angry at people who hurt you, say it all to God, leave the judging with him, and look to the cross, where Jesus prayed for his enemies.

lament: a compact example of the lament form

psalms.line: In five short verses a poor and needy person begs God to hurry to help him, and still stops to pray that all who seek God would rejoice.
psalms.guide: Some prayers have no time for long words; a plea for God to hurry is a full prayer, for a hospital corridor or a sleepless night. Notice that even this urgent prayer stops to think of others who seek God.

psalms.line: An aging believer who has trusted God since birth prays not to be cast off when his strength fails, and longs to tell the next generation of God's power.
psalms.guide: If you are old, this is your prayer: you may fear weakness and being set aside, and say verse 9 to God. Verse 18 says you still have work to do. If you care for someone old, the psalm asks you to be part of God's answer: visit, and listen.

psalms.line: A prayer that God give the king justice, so that he defends the poor and needy and his rule brings peace from sea to sea; Book Two ends here with a doxology.
psalms.guide: The first test of a ruler here is how he treats the poor and those with no helper, and that test applies to anyone with power: a parent, a boss, a leader in a church. Ask whether the weakest people near you find you fair, and whose life you have treated as cheap.

psalms.line: Asaph nearly lost his footing envying the prosperous wicked, until he entered God's sanctuary; he ends confessing that God holds his hand and is his portion forever.
psalms.guide: Name where envy has caught you, as this psalm does, and keep talking to God about it. Take your hardest questions into worship with God's people. If faith feels as if it is slipping, hold on to verse 23, and pray verse 25 slowly, asking God to make it true of you.

people: The psalm is a communal lament

psalms.line: The community cries over a sanctuary smashed and burned, asks why God has rejected his flock, and remembers him as King from ancient times; the psalm ends unanswered.
psalms.guide: If you have stood in a ruin, a marriage, a church, a home, a hope, describe the damage to God in detail; you do not have to tidy your grief first. Remind God of his own promises, as verse 2 does. The psalm ends with its question open, and you may stop with yours open too.

psalms.line: The people give thanks, and God answers that at the time he chooses he will judge fairly; honor comes from him alone.
psalms.guide: Ask where you are trying to lift your own horn; honor comes from God, not from the right connections. If you are waiting for wrongs to be put right, hear verse 2: God chooses the time, so the waiting is not wasted and the last word is his.

psalms.line: God dwells in Zion and has broken the weapons of war there; he rises to judge and to save the lowly of the earth.
psalms.guide: Ask what weapons you trust, and which are aimed at you; God is stronger than both. The psalm gives the victory to God and to the lowly, not to any modern army or nation. If you made a promise to God in a hard time, keep it now, as verse 11 asks.

lament: Still others treat it as a timeless lament

psalms.line: Sleepless and beyond comfort, the psalmist asks whether God has rejected his people forever, then resolves to remember, and recalls the path through the sea whose footprints no one saw.
psalms.guide: You may pray its questions as your own; a temple singer prayed them through the night. Then do what he did and turn to what God has done. You may not see God's footprints in your life now, and the psalm says that was true even at the sea.

psalms.line: Asaph retells Israel's story for the next generation: again and again the people forgot and rebelled, and again and again God judged and showed mercy, until he chose David the shepherd.
psalms.guide: Ask who your next generation is, and tell them the story honestly, with the failures left in. Then read your own life the same way: where you forgot what God did, and where he has still been leading you.

people: The psalm is a communal lament

psalms.line: The nations have left Jerusalem in ruins with the dead unburied; the people ask how long, plead for forgiveness for the sake of God's name, and pray for the captives.
psalms.guide: If you have seen what was precious torn down, bring God your grief and your anger, and your own sins in the same breath. Pray for the captives of verse 11 in our own world: those in prison, in war, with no one to speak for them.

people: Psalm 80 is the third communal lament in Book III

psalms.line: The people pray to the Shepherd of Israel to restore them; the vine he brought out of Egypt lies broken and burned, and three times they ask him to make his face shine on them.
psalms.guide: If you have watched something God planted get broken down, a family, a church, a friendship, ask him why and ask him to come back to what is his. Learn the refrain of verses 3, 7 and 19, which asks for God's face before anything else.

psalms.line: A festival call to worship breaks into God's own voice: he freed his people from slavery, he grieves that they would not listen, and he longs to feed them with the finest wheat.
psalms.guide: Hear God's side of the story: he says if only, twice, and wants to fill your mouth with good things. Ask where you are not listening, perhaps in the middle of worship, when he most wants you to stop and hear.

psalms.line: God puts the powers that rule the world on trial for judging unjustly, commands them to defend the weak and the fatherless, and the psalmist asks God himself to judge the earth.
psalms.guide: Anyone with power over others, a parent, a boss, a teacher, a pastor, will answer to God for how the weak were treated; ask who near you has no one to speak for them. When the courts and the powerful fail, pray verse 8, which hands justice to the one judge who will not fail.

psalms.line: The psalmist begs God not to stay silent while the surrounding nations plot against Israel, and ends hoping that they will come to know the LORD alone as Most High.
psalms.guide: When you feel surrounded, you may ask God not to be silent. But let the ending shape what you want: not that those against you vanish, but that they come to know the LORD. Can you pray that for the people who stand against you?

zion: Psalm 84 is often classed as a Song of Zion

psalms.line: A worshiper aches for the courts of the LORD, blesses those whose hearts are set on the pilgrim roads, and says one day in God's courts is better than a thousand elsewhere.
psalms.guide: If you ache for God, that is not a fault but a sign you were made for him. The road may run through a valley of tears, as verse 6 says, and those whose strength is in God find springs there. Take one small step toward God's presence this week.

people: The psalm is a communal lament

psalms.line: Remembering past mercy, the people ask God to revive them again, and a voice listens and hears a promise of peace: loving devotion and faithfulness meet, righteousness and peace kiss.
psalms.guide: If you have known God's mercy before and find yourself in trouble again, pray from that place: remember past mercy and ask for it again. Notice verse 8, where someone chose to listen before the promises came.

psalms.line: In distress, David calls on the Lord as a poor and needy servant, grounds his plea in God's kindness and loving devotion, and asks for an undivided heart.
psalms.guide: Pray verse 11 slowly; most of us are pulled many ways at once. In trouble, pray God's own words back to him as this psalm does: read Exodus 34:6 aloud and ask him to be to you what he says he is.

zion: Psalm 87 is a brief hymn of Zion

psalms.line: God loves the gates of Zion and records Israel's old enemies and distant peoples among those born there; all their springs of joy are in her.
psalms.guide: God can write a new birthplace beside a name, and people once far off can be counted as his own. The psalm speaks of God's city, not of any modern state or border; let it soften the way you see people from other nations.

psalms.line: A man who has suffered since his youth cries to God day and night from the edge of death, his friends gone; the psalm never turns to trust, and it ends in darkness.
psalms.guide: Psalm 88 does not ask you to feel anything; it gives words to someone already in the dark, or sitting beside someone who is. Let it stand as it is, without rushing to a happier ending, and pray it as your own; the prayer still counts. If you are not in the dark, pray it for someone who is.

psalms.line: The psalm sings of God's loving devotion and his sworn covenant with David, then turns: the king is rejected and his crown in the dust, and it asks where that love has gone. Book Three ends with a blessing.
psalms.guide: Set down what is true of God before facing what hurts, as verses 1 to 18 do. If you hold a promise that seems to have fallen apart, say the promise aloud, say what has happened, ask where his love has gone, and if you can, bless him anyway, as the last verse does, with the question still open.

people: Psalm 90 is a communal lament with strong wisdom features

psalms.line: A prayer headed with Moses' name sets the eternal God, his people's home in every generation, against the shortness of human life, and asks God to teach us to number our days.
psalms.guide: Start where the psalm starts, with God as home before the mountains were born. Pray verse 12 each day; people who know their days are few often learn what matters most. Let verse 14 shape your mornings: before the day's work, ask God to satisfy you with his love.

psalms.line: The safety of the one who dwells in the shelter of the Most High, covered by his wings in plague and terror, ending with God's own promise to be with him in trouble.
psalms.guide: Pray it for real dangers, the surgery, the night shift, the long drive, but as trust and not as a charm; the shelter is a person. It is not a promise that no believer is ever harmed, and never a reason to refuse a doctor or ordinary care. Hold the promise of verse 15, God with you in trouble, whatever the outcome.

psalms.line: A song for the Sabbath: it is good to praise the LORD morning and night, and the righteous, planted in God's house, still bear fruit in old age.
psalms.guide: Rest is not only stopping work; it is gladness at what God has done. Let verse 14 encourage anyone growing old: people rooted in God still bear fruit in prayer, wisdom and kindness.

praise: Psalm 93 is a hymn of God's kingship

psalms.line: The LORD reigns, robed in majesty; the floods lift up their roar, and the LORD on high is mightier than them all.
psalms.guide: Name the floods roaring in your life; the psalm does not say the waters are quiet, only that God is higher still. Say its first words aloud when you are afraid, not as a feeling but as a fact to stand on while the waves still pound.

psalms.line: A cry to the Judge of the earth against the proud who crush widows, foreigners and orphans and say God does not see; it ends with testimony that God's loving devotion held the psalmist up.
psalms.guide: Ask who the widows, foreigners and fatherless are in your town; God sees how they are treated. If anxiety is overwhelming you, verse 19 names it without shame: bring it to God, who comforts, and if worry has become too heavy, tell someone you trust, a friend, a pastor or a doctor.

psalms.line: A call to sing and kneel before the great King who made the sea and the dry land, broken by God's own warning not to harden their hearts as their ancestors did.
psalms.guide: Move from loud joy to quiet kneeling; if you only ever do one, try the other this week. Today is the word that matters: if you hear God's voice in Scripture, in conscience or in a friend's honest word, do not harden your heart.

psalms.line: The whole earth is called to sing a new song and tell the nations of God's glory, and sea, field and forest rejoice because the LORD comes to judge the world in righteousness.
psalms.guide: Sing the new song of something God has done that you have not yet thanked him for. Then see his judgment from the side of the poor and the wronged, for whom a fair judge is the best news there is.

psalms.line: The LORD reigns, appearing in cloud and fire; idols are put to shame, and those who love him are called to hate evil and rejoice.
psalms.guide: Hold awe and joy together: God is fearsome, and he is the reason the righteous rejoice. Carry verse 11 into a dark week; the light it promises may start small, like seed, and grow.

psalms.line: A new song for the LORD's victory: all the earth shouts with lyre and horn, and the rivers clap their hands, because he is coming to judge the world with righteousness.
psalms.guide: Ask what God has done that deserves a new song from you, and let joy be loud sometimes. Let the clapping rivers remind you that the world is waiting for its King, and praise him with it.

psalms.line: The LORD reigns from Zion, a King who loves justice; he answered Moses, Aaron and Samuel, forgave and still dealt with wrong, and three times the psalm says that he is holy.
psalms.guide: Ask whether you approach God casually or as the holy King; the psalm holds both, he is holy and he answers. Ask who prays for you as Moses and Samuel prayed for their people, and whom you are praying for.

psalms.line: The whole earth is called to come before the LORD with singing and enter his gates with thanks, because he made us, we are his, and his loving devotion endures forever.
psalms.guide: Come into God's presence by the simple door of thanks: before you ask for anything, thank him for one thing, then another. Let verse 3 settle you on a hard day as much as an easy one: you belong to someone, and he is good.

psalms.line: A king's vow of integrity: to walk in his own house with a whole heart, keep worthless things from his eyes, and refuse slander and pride at his court.
psalms.guide: You have a house too: a home, a workplace, a set of friends, a screen. Ask what you set before your eyes there and what talk you allow. Begin with your own heart, and pray the question of verse 2, since integrity is not built alone.

lament: Psalm 102 breaks into the praise of Book IV with a raw lament

psalms.line: A prayer headed for one who is afflicted: his days vanish like smoke, he cannot eat, he is alone like a bird on a roof, and then he turns to the LORD whose years never end.
psalms.guide: This psalm was written for your worst day; its heading says so. Pour out your complaint in its words or your own, then look up from your short days to God, who remains the same. It does not say the suffering ends at once, only that God does not despise the prayer of the destitute.

psalms.line: The psalmist tells his own soul to bless the LORD and forget none of his benefits: forgiveness, healing, redemption, compassion like a father's, and sins removed as far as east from west.
psalms.guide: Talk to your own soul as the psalm does and name, one by one, what God has done; gratitude is often a choice to remember before it is a feeling. Leave your sins where God put them. If you are ill, verse 3 is no reason to refuse medical care, and no sign that your faith has failed.

psalms.line: A hymn of wonder at the Creator who stretches out the heavens, waters the valleys, feeds every creature, and gives breath to all that lives.
psalms.guide: Look at the sky, a storm, the edge of the sea, and start where the psalm starts, with God's greatness. Thank him by name for the ordinary gifts on your table. Take one slow breath and thank him for it, since every breath is his.

psalms.line: A call to give thanks becomes a retelling of Israel's story as God keeping his promise to Abraham, from Joseph in chains to the exodus and the land.
psalms.guide: Look back at your life and ask what God remembered: where were you small and unprotected, and kept anyway? Tell someone. If you are in a long, hard chapter, remember that Joseph's feet were in chains before his story turned. Then read Psalm 106 beside it.

psalms.line: The same story told as confession: the people have sinned like their ancestors, again and again God handed them over and rescued them, and Book Four ends with a plea to be gathered.
psalms.guide: Learn to say we about sin, rather than blaming those before you or beside you. Then find the word that saves the story in verse 44: God heard and remembered. Confess your own repeated failures, and trust the God who still hears.

psalms.line: Four scenes of rescue, the lost in the desert, prisoners in chains, the sick near death and sailors in a storm; each cries to the LORD, is rescued, and is called to give thanks.
psalms.guide: Thanks is meant to be spoken aloud, so if you have been rescued, say so; someone may need to hear it. If you are in a storm now, tell God plainly. The psalm is not a promise that every prayer is answered the same way, and the same book keeps Psalm 88.

psalms.line: An old song sung again: the psalmist wakes the dawn with music, recalls an old word from God, and confesses that human help is worthless and God will win the battle.
psalms.guide: A steadfast heart is not the same as calm circumstances; in Psalm 57 the same words came from a cave. You may borrow old prayers for your own day; a prayer learned long ago may be exactly the one you need now.

lament: The psalm is an individual lament

psalms.line: A man falsely accused by people he had loved brings the wound to God, words and all; a long curse follows, and he ends praising the God who stands at the right hand of the needy.
psalms.guide: Anger told to God is safer than anger acted on. Under all the accusation he says, in verse 4, that he is a man of prayer: keep praying, and leave the judging to God. Some readers take verses 6 to 19 as the enemies' curse, which he quotes. Either way, follow the psalm from the courtroom to praise, toward verse 31.

psalms.line: The LORD invites the king to sit at his right hand and swears that he is a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek; it is the Old Testament text the New Testament quotes most often about Christ.
psalms.guide: Ask whether your picture of Jesus has grown small: a teacher, a helper, but not Lord. Christians live in the until of verse 1, when not everything is put right yet. If you find it hard to pray, verse 4 says there is someone who prays for you, whose priesthood does not end.

psalms.line: A short alphabetic hymn of thanks for God's works, his provision and his covenant, ending with the saying that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.
psalms.guide: Ponder slowly what God has done, in the Bible's story and in your own. Ask whether you have begun where wisdom begins: not with cleverness, a degree or experience, but with the fear of the LORD.

psalms.line: The blessed person who fears the LORD: generous, just, steady in the face of bad news, with a heart fixed on God.
psalms.guide: Steadiness here comes from trust, not from having no trouble. Ask whether what you have is open-handed, like seed scattered on a field; generosity is part of what it means to fear the LORD.

praise: The psalm is a hymn of praise in three parts

psalms.line: The LORD is high above the nations, yet he stoops to lift the poor from the dust and gives the childless woman a home; the Hallel sung at the great festivals begins here.
psalms.guide: Ask where you look for greatness; God's is shown in how far down he reaches. Ask who is in the dust in your town, and whether you are willing to stoop with him.

psalms.line: The exodus as a song: the sea flees, the Jordan turns back, the mountains skip like rams, and the earth trembles before the God who turns rock into springs of water.
psalms.guide: See God's great acts with fresh eyes, as if you were watching the hills jump. Where the ground of your life feels like flint, remember who he is, the one who can bring water out of stone, without demanding how he will act.

psalms.line: Glory belongs to God's name, not ours: Israel's God is in heaven, idols of silver and gold can neither see nor speak, and all who fear the LORD are called to trust him.
psalms.guide: Anything we trust to save us or make us worth something can work like an idol: money, success, a person, a cause, a screen. Verse 8 asks what you are becoming like. Pray verse 1 slowly, and often.

psalms.line: A person rescued from the edge of death loves the LORD who heard him, tells his soul to return to rest, and lifts the cup of salvation before God's people.
psalms.guide: Answered prayer is not the end of prayer but a reason for more. When your heart still races after a hard time, say verse 7 to yourself. Is there a rescue you have never thanked God for aloud?

praise: The psalm has the shape of a complete hymn in miniature

psalms.line: The shortest psalm calls every nation to praise the LORD for his great loving devotion and his everlasting faithfulness.
psalms.guide: Learn it by heart in a minute. Then let it widen your picture of God's people: no nation is left out of its call, and none is above it.

psalms.line: The Hallel ends with thanks for a love that endures forever: a leader pushed to the edge of death is rescued, the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone, and the crowd blesses the one who comes in the LORD's name.
psalms.guide: People do not have the last word over someone God holds. If you have been brought through something, tell what God did. If you have been the rejected stone, the verdict of others is not the last one.

wisdom: Although the psalm is often called a wisdom or Torah psalm

psalms.line: The longest psalm: twenty-two stanzas of eight verses, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, praying through affliction to understand, love and keep God's word, and ending as a lost sheep asking to be sought.
psalms.guide: You do not need to read it in one sitting: a stanza a day takes twenty-two days, and the slow reading here gives you one stanza at a time. If you feel only duty, ask for delight. And let the last verse be yours: when you stray, do not try harder alone; ask to be sought.

lament: The psalm is a short individual lament

psalms.line: The first Song of Ascents begins far from home among liars: the psalmist wants peace, and those around him want war.
psalms.guide: Many people start toward God because they are worn out by where they are; say so to God. This is the first step of a longer road, and the next psalms go up to Jerusalem.

psalms.line: A traveler looks to the hills and asks where help will come from: from the LORD, Maker of heaven and earth, who never sleeps and keeps his going out and his coming in.
psalms.guide: Ask where you look first for help, and look past it to the one who made the hills. Pray it over someone you love as they set out, or over yourself facing a long road. It does not promise that no harm will ever come.

psalms.line: A pilgrim glad to be invited to the house of the LORD stands inside Jerusalem's gates and calls for prayer for its peace.
psalms.guide: Ask whether worship with God's people is something you are glad to go to, who invited you, and whom you might invite. Pray for the peace of Jerusalem and everyone who lives there, and for your own town and the people hardest to love; prayer for peace leads to work for peace.

people: Psalm 123 is a brief communal lament

psalms.line: As servants watch their master's hand, the people look to the LORD and plead for mercy, worn out by the scorn of the proud.
psalms.guide: If you have been on the receiving end of contempt, the psalm does not ask you to pretend it does not hurt. Turn your eyes from the scornful to God's hand, and keep watching until mercy comes.

psalms.line: The people say aloud what would have happened without the LORD on their side: they escaped like a bird from a torn net, and their help is in his name.
psalms.guide: Finish the psalm's opening line about your own life: where would you be? Most people can name a moment when the net tore. Say it aloud, together, so that the next generation knows.

psalms.line: Those who trust the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be shaken, and he surrounds his people as the mountains surround Jerusalem.
psalms.guide: You are steady not because you are strong but because God is around you. When unjust people hold power for a long time, it is easy to copy them; ask where you are tempted to reach for what is wrong because that seems to be how things work now.

psalms.line: The people remember when the LORD restored them and joy seemed a dream, then pray for restoration again, trusting that sowing in tears ends in a harvest of joy.
psalms.guide: If you are doing the right thing with no joy in it and no harvest in sight, the psalm does not call your tears wrong: the weeping farmer keeps sowing. If God has done great things for you before, tell them again; old joy feeds new hope.

wisdom: it is usually classed as a wisdom psalm

psalms.line: Building and guarding are in vain unless the LORD builds and guards; he gives sleep to those he loves, and children are a heritage from him.
psalms.guide: Work without God is in vain, and worry is not the same as work; lying down to rest can be an act of trust. If you have children, hold them as gifts in trust, arrows made to be sent out. The psalm's praise of children is no promise of a child to everyone who prays for one.

psalms.line: Happy is everyone who fears the LORD: work that feeds you, a table with people around it, grandchildren, a city at peace, and a blessing from Zion.
psalms.guide: Notice these ordinary goods as gifts when you have them. If your table looks different from the one in verse 3, the blessing of verse 5 is still for you; pray it over your own home and the homes around you.

psalms.line: Israel says it has been attacked since its youth, its back plowed like a field, yet its enemies never prevailed, because the LORD cut the cords of the wicked.
psalms.guide: Many people carry long scars from years of mistreatment. The psalm does not call the wounds small, but it says the cords were cut. Look back and name where God brought an end to something that might have destroyed you.

psalms.line: From the depths the psalmist cries to the LORD; if God kept a record of sins no one could stand, but with him there is forgiveness, so he waits more than watchmen wait for morning.
psalms.guide: If you fear your wrongs are too many, verses 3 and 4 say God does not keep score that way. Pray verse 1 from wherever you are. The psalm does not promise when the morning comes, only that it will; when you find hope in the depths, pass it on.

psalms.line: Three verses: a heart that is not proud, a soul calmed and quieted like a weaned child with its mother, and a call for Israel to hope in the LORD.
psalms.guide: Set down some of the questions too big for you, and some of the ambitions you have been grabbing at. The psalm does not say they do not matter; it says you can be quiet with God while they wait.

psalms.line: The psalm remembers David's vow to find a dwelling place for God and the ark brought to Zion, and answers with God's oath: a son of David on the throne, and Zion his resting place.
psalms.guide: Ask what it would mean to care about God's presence that much, in your home, your church and your town. God answers a promise with a bigger promise; bring him what little you can.

wisdom: Psalm 133 is a short wisdom psalm

psalms.line: The goodness of brothers living together in unity, like oil running down Aaron's beard and dew falling on Zion, where the LORD commands his blessing.
psalms.guide: Unity among God's people is a joy and not only a duty. Ask where there is a quarrel in your family or church that you could help to heal, and pray for unity as a gift that runs down from above.

liturgy: Psalm 134 is a short liturgy of three verses

psalms.line: The last Song of Ascents calls the LORD's servants who stand in his house by night to lift their hands and bless him, and blesses them in return.
psalms.guide: Some service is done at night, unseen: a parent with a sick child, a nurse on a late shift, someone praying awake. God sees night work, and it can be worship. Speak the blessing of verse 3 over someone else.

praise: Psalm 135 is a hymn of praise

psalms.line: A call to praise the God who chose Israel and acts in storm and exodus, set beside idols of silver and gold that cannot speak, see or hear.
psalms.guide: Praise does not have to be new to be true; this psalm is made of older words, and they can become yours. Say aloud what you know about God from his word and from your own life.

psalms.line: Twenty-six lines, each answered by the same refrain, thank the LORD from creation through the exodus to the food he gives every creature: his loving devotion endures forever.
psalms.guide: Read it aloud with someone, one of you reading each line and the other answering. Then answer each part of your own story with the refrain, and notice verse 25: every meal is a line in this psalm.

psalms.line: Exiles in Babylon weep by its rivers and cannot sing the LORD's song; they swear never to forget Jerusalem and cry to God for justice, ending in the hardest lines in the Psalms.
psalms.guide: It honors grief and does not hurry the exiles to cheer up; you are allowed to hang up your harp for a while. If you carry rage at what was done to you or to someone you love, take it to God out loud instead of acting on it, and leave the judging to him. Its last lines are a prayer spoken to God, never a word to be turned against any people or any person.

thanks: Psalm 138 is an individual song of thanksgiving

psalms.line: David thanks the LORD with his whole heart because God answered on the day he called and strengthened him, and trusts God to fulfill his purpose for him.
psalms.guide: Sometimes God's answer is not to remove the trouble but to give courage inside it. On a hard day, borrow verse 8; when you are unsure of it, pray its last line: you are his work.

wisdom: Psalm 139 is often classed as a wisdom or meditative psalm

psalms.line: God knows David completely, there is nowhere to flee from his presence, he formed him in the womb, and the psalm ends asking God to search his heart and lead him in the everlasting way.
psalms.guide: God knows the worst about you and has not let go; if you have tried to run, read verses 7 to 12 slowly. You were made with care, and so was every other person. End the day with verses 23 and 24, letting God look at you first.

psalms.line: David asks to be rescued from violent men whose tongues are poisonous as snakes, and trusts that the LORD upholds justice for the poor.
psalms.guide: If you have been hurt by slander or a lie that spread, take the hurt to God, who knows that words can poison. Stand where verse 12 stands, with the poor and needy. And ask whether your own words heal or harm.

psalms.line: An evening prayer that rises like incense: guard my mouth, keep my heart from evil, and let the righteous correct me as a kindness.
psalms.guide: Use it at the end of the day, asking God to guard your mouth and your heart. Verse 5 asks something hard: can you take correction from a good friend as a kindness, rather than prefer to be flattered?

lament: Psalm 142 is a short individual lament

psalms.line: Hiding in a cave, David pours out his complaint: his spirit is faint, no one cares for his life, and the LORD is his refuge and his portion.
psalms.guide: Pour out your complaint without tidying it up; you may say honestly that no one cares. Then look at the end, where he hopes the righteous will gather around him again, and ask who is in a cave right now with no one at their right hand.

psalms.line: Crushed and sitting in darkness, David pleads on God's faithfulness rather than his own, since no one alive is righteous before God, and asks to hear of his loving devotion in the morning.
psalms.guide: It is a model of prayer from the bottom of a hard time: it confesses, remembers, reaches out, and asks to be taught. Pick one of its short prayers, from verses 7, 8 or 10, and pray it today.

psalms.line: David blesses the LORD his Rock, marvels that God regards fleeting human beings, asks for rescue, and pictures a people at peace whose God is the LORD.
psalms.guide: When you feel as small as a breath, remember that God stoops to think of you. Then ask what your picture of a good life is; the psalm ends with full barns and quiet streets, and says the real blessing is having the LORD as your God.

praise: Psalm 145 is a hymn of praise

psalms.line: An alphabet of praise to God as King: great, gracious and compassionate, near to all who call on him, lifting all who are bowed down.
psalms.guide: Praise here is a daily practice, not a mood. Tell the next generation what God has done. If you are bowed down, verse 14 is for you; if you feel far from God, verse 18 says you need only call, without fine words.

psalms.line: A vow to praise the LORD for life and a warning not to trust princes, whose plans die with them; the LORD reigns forever and cares for the oppressed, the hungry, the prisoner, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow.
psalms.guide: Ask where you place your hope: a leader, a movement, a person with power. The psalm says they cannot save, and that they will die. Look at the people God cares for in verses 7 to 9; if you belong to him, they are your concern too.

psalms.line: The God who counts the stars heals the brokenhearted, rebuilds Jerusalem, feeds the ravens, sends snow and thaw, and gives his word to his people.
psalms.guide: If your heart is broken, verse 3 is for you: the God who named the stars binds up wounds. If you are in a cold season, the psalm says his word still runs swiftly, and the waters will flow again.

psalms.line: Everything above and everything below, angels, sun and stars, sea creatures, weather, mountains, kings and children, is called to praise the LORD who made them.
psalms.guide: Look up tonight; the sky praises God by being what he made it to be. You are in a choir with whales, hailstorms and kings. Invite someone old or young to praise with you.

psalms.line: A new song for the God who delights in his people and crowns the humble, then a picture of the faithful with praise in their mouths and a sword in their hands.
psalms.guide: Sing praise that is fresh, not routine: what has God done lately that you have not thanked him for? For a Christian, the plain notes say, the sword is God's word, to be spoken with truth and love.

psalms.line: The last psalm: praise God in his sanctuary and his heavens, for his mighty acts, with every instrument, and let everything that has breath praise the LORD.
psalms.guide: You do not need to feel like praising to begin; many of the psalms before this one began in the dark. Add your breath to the sound. Jews and Christians still pray and sing the Psalms every day, and the last word of the book can be yours too.
